content: The prevalence of asthma varies significantly across different geographical regions, and observational studies have proposed that dietary sodium intake might influence asthma. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of dietary sodium manipulation on asthma control. A comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Airways Group asthma register, and additional studies were identified by reviewing the bibliographies of included randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The most recent search was completed in November 2010. Only RCTs that investigated the effects of either dietary sodium reduction or increased sodium intake in individuals with asthma were included in the analysis. Two reviewers independently assessed the studies and extracted the relevant data. Statistical analyses were performed using RevMan 5, employing mean differences and random effects models. A total of nine studies were identified that examined the relationship between sodium manipulation and asthma. Of these, five studies involved individuals with asthma (318 participants), and four studies focused on individuals with exercise-induced asthma (63 participants). The findings revealed no significant benefits of dietary sodium restriction on overall asthma control. However, in the studies involving exercise-induced asthma, there was limited evidence suggesting that a low-sodium diet might improve lung function following exercise and potentially enhance baseline lung function. It is important to note that these findings were derived from a very small number of participants. In conclusion, this review did not find any substantial evidence to support the notion that dietary sodium reduction significantly improves asthma control. While there may be some improvements in lung function associated with a low-sodium diet in cases of exercise-induced asthma, the clinical relevance of these effects remains uncertain.
